title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: DTE wants two new gas plants for surging data center demand—what it means for bills and the grid.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Friday morning, August 28, and today we're digging into DTE's push for two new natural gas plants to meet the electricity hunger from data centers.
That lead story feels like the biggest shift we've seen in a while. Graham, walk us through what DTE is actually asking regulators for.
DTE Energy plans to seek approval for two new gas-fired plants because data centers are driving up demand fast in southeast Michigan.
Why now? We've heard about coal retirements for years, but how does this connect directly to the data center boom?
The timing lines up with older coal units coming offline while hyperscale projects keep landing in the region. DTE says the plants are needed to keep the lights on and the grid reliable.
And if approved, how much could this actually raise customer bills? The summary mentions it could push rates up.
Exactly. Residents from Detroit all the way to Ann Arbor would feel it through higher electric rates, plus we'd be locking in more fossil fuel generation for years.
What about the bigger picture on water use? Gas plants need cooling water too, right? How does that stack up against the data centers themselves?
It's another layer. Data centers already draw huge amounts for cooling, and adding gas plants could compound the strain on local supplies, especially in areas already watching aquifer levels.
Farmland and towns are in the mix as well. Where might these plants go, and what kind of pushback are we seeing from communities?
Siting fights are heating up across the same suburbs that are rewriting zoning rules today. Homeowners worry about noise, traffic, and property values even 30 miles out.
This feels like part of a longer battle. How many townships have already hit pause on data centers while they figure out the rules?
Several across the state, from Solon Township extending its freeze yesterday to Garfield Township's year-long halt earlier this week. It's a pattern of local governments buying time.
What happens next with the DTE request? Is there a clear timeline for public hearings or a decision from regulators?
The company will file with the Michigan Public Service Commission, and that process usually includes comment periods where residents and local officials can weigh in.
So the stakes are real for everyday ratepayers. If these plants get built, we're looking at higher bills and more emissions for the foreseeable future.
That's the core tension right now between economic growth from data centers and the costs passed down to households.
Let's shift to some of the other developments from today. Two more Metro Detroit towns are changing their zoning after resident complaints.
Yes, local officials in two additional suburbs are updating codes specifically to address noise, water use, and power strain from potential projects.
How might that ripple out to homeowners farther away?
It could slow or block large developments that developers had in mind, which in turn might affect property values and utility costs across a wider area.
And in Wixom, a developer is suing the city after its project got blocked.
That's right. The firm claims the zoning decisions unfairly killed its plans, and the lawsuit could end up costing taxpayers if it moves forward.
What are people in Oakland County watching for in that case?
Whether it chills future investment or gives neighborhoods stronger protections against heavy industrial loads.
Yesterday we had two more extensions on moratoriums. Solon Township is keeping its freeze through early next year.
Leaders there recommended extending the existing moratorium while they update zoning to tackle noise, traffic, and utility costs.
And a West Michigan community did the same, pushing its ban out to at least early 2027.
Residents there get more time to study power demand, noise, and water use before anything moves ahead.
Gaines Township is taking a different approach with actual sound measurements.
Officials will measure decibel levels at a proposed site to see how much neighbors would hear from cooling fans and generators.
That could be a game-changer if the numbers exceed local limits.
Homeowners within a few miles now have concrete data to judge the impact on daily life.
From earlier this week, township supervisors across northern Michigan backed state bills to make data centers pay more for grid upgrades.
The idea is that forcing operators to cover more of those costs could keep residential bills lower, but only if local governments retain leverage.
Garfield Township also voted to pause new proposals for a full year.
Supervisors want time to research limits on power, water, and noise in Grand Traverse County before any big projects file applications.
Lowell Township is still working on its own ordinance after months of debate.
The rules they're hammering out will decide where facilities can locate and what caps apply to power and noise in Kent County.
And there's a new state proposal requiring data centers to disclose their water use.
That would give communities hard numbers on aquifer and municipal supply strain before projects get approved.
So across the board, local pushback is growing while the state level sees more disclosure and cost-sharing ideas.
It shows how quickly the conversation has shifted from welcoming investment to managing the downsides.
On deck for listeners, are there any meetings coming up that people can attend?
No major public hearings are listed for today or tomorrow in the tracker, but several townships like Solon and Garfield are in active zoning rewrite phases.
Folks should check their local township websites or the Michigan Data Center Tracker map for any last-minute notices.
That's the practical next step while the bigger regulatory fights play out.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: DTE Gas Plants and the Data Center Power Crunch
